110:
Something is absorbing when it is so deeply interesting and engaging that it takes over your complete attention — not just some of it, but all of it. When you experience something absorbing, your mind gets fully drawn into it, and the rest of the world seems to fade away. You might forget what time it is, lose track of where you are, or completely forget you had something else to do.

Think of a sponge soaking up water — it takes in every single drop, leaving nothing behind. An absorbing experience works the same way on your mind: it soaks up your entire focus and holds it there.

The defining quality of something absorbing is total mental immersion. You are not passively noticing it or casually enjoying it — you are in it, fully. You can recognize this feeling because you look up and realize hours have passed, you feel genuinely reluctant or even unable to stop, distractions around you stop registering, and when the experience ends, you need a moment to "come back" to the real world.
What kinds of things can be absorbing?

The word is used broadly for almost any experience that holds the mind completely.

A book with a compelling plot and rich characters can be absorbing. A film that keeps your eyes on the screen from the very first minute to the last can be absorbing. A conversation so deep and meaningful that neither person notices the time passing is absorbing. A puzzle, a game, or a difficult problem at work can be absorbing when it fully engages your mental energy. A lecture or a live performance that commands your undivided focus is absorbing too.

The common thread is always the same: the thing holds your whole mind, not just a corner of it.

"Absorbing" is a strong word — noticeably stronger than "interesting" or "enjoyable." If something is simply interesting, it gets your attention and makes you curious. If it is absorbing, it does far more — it captures your full mental presence and holds it completely. A useful way to feel the difference: you might glance at something interesting, but you get genuinely lost in something absorbing.
How it compares to similar words

Several words are close to "absorbing," and understanding the differences sharpens your feel for this word.

Engaging is milder — it draws your interest and keeps it, but does not necessarily take over your entire mind. Gripping focuses more on tension and suspense, and feels most natural when talking about thrillers, dramas, or high-stakes situations. Captivating suggests being held almost like a spell, and often carries a sense of beauty or charm. Fascinating suggests something fills you with wonder and curiosity — you can be fascinated even by a single surprising fact. Riveting is very close to absorbing, but with a stronger sense of dramatic intensity, almost as if you are physically nailed to the spot.

What makes "absorbing" special is that it captures full mental immersion cleanly and generally — without any specific leaning toward tension, beauty, or wonder. It is the purest, most neutral word for something that takes your mind completely.

Almost always positive. To call something absorbing is to compliment it. You are saying it is exceptional at holding attention, which is high praise for a book, a film, a game, or any experience. In rare cases it can carry a faintly neutral tone — for example, if someone is so absorbed in their work that they neglect everything else — but that depends entirely on context and is not the typical use.

"Absorbing" has a slightly literary or intellectual flavor. It is the kind of word you find in book reviews, film critiques, and thoughtful discussions. It is not informal slang, but it is not stiff or old-fashioned either. It fits naturally in written essays, academic settings, and everyday conversation among educated speakers.

"The biography was one of the most absorbing books she had ever read."

"Despite its three-hour length, the film was completely absorbing."

"He found the research so absorbing that he worked straight through the night."

"Their conversation became so absorbing that they missed their bus entirely."

"The chess game grew increasingly absorbing as the positions grew more complex."

In one sentence: absorbing means so interesting and engaging that it takes over your full attention and immerses your mind completely — the highest natural compliment you can pay to anything designed to hold your interest.
111:
Absorption is the process of one thing drawing something inside itself — taking it in fully, so that what was outside becomes part of what's inside.

The keyword here is inside. Absorption isn't just contact, or collection, or coating. It's genuine entry — something passes through and becomes incorporated.

The classic image: a dry sponge dropped in water. The water doesn't sit on top of it — it enters the sponge, fills its tiny spaces, becomes part of it. That's absorption. The sponge has absorbed the water.
Absorption of Liquids and Gases (Everyday Physical Sense)

In the most common, everyday sense, absorption is when a material soaks up a liquid or gas.

A paper towel absorbs a spill. Soil absorbs rainwater. Dry bread absorbs soup. Your skin absorbs lotion. In each case, the liquid doesn't merely rest on the surface — it enters the material and spreads throughout it.

This is also what distinguishes absorption from simple contact. When water beads up on a waxed surface and rolls off, that's the opposite of absorption. When a cloth draws the water in and holds it, that's absorption.
Absorption of Energy (Light, Sound, Heat, Radiation)

Absorption isn't limited to liquids and gases. Forms of energy — light, heat, sound, radiation — can also be absorbed.

Light: When sunlight hits a dark surface, most of the light is absorbed — it enters the material and is converted into heat rather than bouncing back. This is why a black car sitting in sunlight gets much hotter than a white one. The black surface absorbs more light energy; the white one reflects more of it away.

Sound: Some materials absorb sound. The sound waves enter the material and their energy is converted into tiny vibrations (heat), rather than bouncing off as an echo. This is the principle behind soundproofing — foam panels and heavy curtains absorb sound rather than reflecting it.

Heat: When you stand in the sun, your skin absorbs heat (thermal energy) from the sun's rays. The energy enters your body.

Radiation: UV radiation from the sun is absorbed by your skin. This is what causes tanning, and why overexposure causes damage — the energy is being taken into the skin's cells.

In every case, the principle is the same: the energy goes in, rather than bouncing away (reflection) or passing straight through (transmission).

In chemistry, absorption has a more precise meaning: it's when one substance — usually a gas or a liquid — is taken into the bulk (the full volume, not just the surface) of another substance.

When carbon dioxide gas dissolves into water, the CO₂ molecules don't just sit on the water's surface. They penetrate throughout the liquid. That's absorption.

Here it's worth knowing about a look-alike word: adsorption (with a "d"). Adsorption is when a substance sticks to the surface of something — a thin coating, not a full entry. The distinction is:

  • Absorption → goes inside
  • Adsorption → clings to the surface

Think of it this way: a sponge absorbs water (the water goes in). A sticky note adsorbs to a wall (it only clings to the outer surface).
Absorption in Biology — How Your Body Takes In Substances

In biology and medicine, absorption refers to the process by which substances cross a biological membrane and enter the bloodstream or cells.

The most important example in your body happens in your small intestine. After you eat, your digestive system breaks food down into its basic components — sugars, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals. These tiny molecules then pass through the cells lining the walls of the small intestine and enter your blood. That passage — from the digestive tract into the bloodstream — is absorption.

From there, your blood carries these nutrients everywhere your body needs them.

Drugs work the same way. When you swallow a tablet, it dissolves in your stomach or intestine, and the medicine is absorbed — it crosses the intestinal wall and enters your blood, which then delivers it to where it needs to act. A medicine described as "poorly absorbed" doesn't cross that membrane efficiently, so only a small amount reaches the bloodstream, reducing its effectiveness.

This is also why doctors sometimes give medicines by injection — injecting a drug directly into a vein bypasses absorption entirely, since the drug is already in the bloodstream.

The skin also absorbs. Medicated creams and patches work by having the drug absorbed through the skin and into the blood beneath. This is called transdermal absorption.
Figurative Absorption — A State of Complete Mental Engagement

Absorption has a powerful figurative meaning too, and it's one you'll encounter very often in writing and conversation.

When a person is absorbed in something, they are so deeply focused on it — so completely engaged — that they are barely aware of anything else around them.

"She read the letter with total absorption."
"The child watched the fire in silent absorption."
"His absorption in the project left no room for distractions."

This meaning is a natural extension of the physical sense. Just as a sponge draws water so fully into itself that there is no separation between the sponge and the water, a person who is absorbed in something has mentally "drawn it in" so completely that, in that moment, their attention and consciousness are entirely occupied by it.

It suggests not just interest, but total immersion. You can be interested in something and still be aware of your surroundings. But when you're absorbed, the outside world fades.
One Thread Through All the Meanings

Whether you're talking about a sponge and water, a wall and sound, a cell and a nutrient, or a mind and a book — absorption always means one thing drawing something else inside itself, fully and genuinely.

Not a surface encounter.
Not a casual collection.
Not a passing touch.

A true taking-in. What was outside is now inside. That is absorption.
112:
To abstain means to deliberately and consciously choose NOT to do something — especially something you could do, might want to do, or are expected to do.

The key idea hidden inside "abstain" is willful self-restraint. You are not simply failing to do something or forgetting to do it. You are actively holding yourself back from it, on purpose.

Think of it this way: if you don't eat breakfast because you overslept, that is not abstaining. But if you wake up, smell the food, feel hungry, and still choose not to eat — that is abstaining.

"Abstain" almost always follows this pattern in a sentence:

Someone abstains from something.

  • She abstained from alcohol.
  • He abstained from voting.
  • They abstained from making any comments.

The word from is its natural partner. You abstain from a thing, not of a thing or on a thing.
The Three Main Situations Where "Abstain" Is Used

1. Abstaining from a substance or activity (personal restraint)

This is about giving up or avoiding something — often something pleasurable, tempting, or habitual — out of willpower, discipline, belief, or principle.

  • A person on a diet might abstain from sugar.
  • A recovering alcoholic abstains from drinking.
  • A monk might abstain from meat for religious reasons.
  • Someone trying to improve their focus might abstain from social media.

In all these cases, the person wants the thing, or at least could have it — but they choose not to. That tension between desire/availability and conscious refusal is the soul of the word.

2. Abstaining in a vote

This is a very specific and important use. In any formal vote — in a parliament, a meeting, a committee, a jury — people usually vote yes or no. But a third option exists: to abstain, which means you are present and eligible to vote, but you deliberately choose neither yes nor nor no.

  • "Ten members voted in favour, four voted against, and two abstained."

Why would someone abstain in a vote? Several reasons:

  • They feel they don't know enough to decide.
  • They have a conflict of interest.
  • They disagree with the entire question being posed.
  • They want to signal disapproval of the process without taking a side.

An abstention is not the same as being absent. The person is there — they just refuse to commit to either side.

3. Abstaining from action in a moral or ethical sense

This usage is slightly more formal and appears in writing, law, philosophy, and serious discourse. It means deliberately refraining from an action, especially when there is a moral or social expectation involved.

  • The judge was asked to abstain from commenting on the ongoing case.
  • Citizens are urged to abstain from violence during protests.
  • Doctors sometimes abstain from offering personal opinions and stick strictly to facts.

Here, the emphasis is on restraint as a responsible or principled choice, especially when speaking or acting could cause harm or bias.
What Makes "Abstain" Different from Similar Words?

Many words mean "not doing something," but abstain is unique because it always carries these features:

  • ✅ The choice is deliberate — not accidental, not forced.
  • ✅ The thing being avoided is available — you could do it.
  • ✅ There is usually effort or willpower involved — it doesn't come easily.
  • ✅ It often implies a principle, belief, discipline, or strategy behind the choice.

Compare:

  • Avoid = stay away from something (could be out of fear or inconvenience, not necessarily willpower).
  • Refrain = hold back from doing something, usually in a specific moment (very close to "abstain," but lighter and less formal; you refrain from laughing in a meeting, but you abstain from alcohol).
  • Forbear = hold back patiently or tolerantly (old-fashioned and rarely used today).
  • Abstain = deliberate, principled, often sustained self-denial; the strongest and most formal of these words.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Abstain" is a formal word. You would see it in:

  • Political reporting ("The senator abstained from the vote.")
  • Health and wellness writing ("Patients are advised to abstain from alcohol before surgery.")
  • Religious contexts ("During the fast, followers abstain from all food until sunset.")
  • Legal and ethical discussions.

In everyday casual conversation, people more often say things like "I'm staying away from sugar" or "I'm not drinking" rather than "I'm abstaining from sugar." But the moment you want to sound precise, serious, or formal, "abstain" is the right word.

Since you're learning this word fully, knowing its noun forms completes the picture:

  • Abstinence — the general state or practice of abstaining, especially over a long period. ("Abstinence from smoking improved his health dramatically.")
  • Abstention — the specific act of abstaining, most commonly used in the context of voting. ("Her abstention in the vote surprised everyone.")

To abstain means to deliberately and consciously hold yourself back from doing something you could do — whether that's consuming a substance, participating in an activity, casting a vote, or taking an action — usually out of discipline, belief, principle, or strategic choice.
113:
Abstemious describes a person who deliberately chooses to eat and drink very little — someone who consciously holds back from overindulging, even when more is freely available. Picture someone at a lavish dinner party who takes small portions, sips just water while everyone else drinks freely, and stops eating well before they're stuffed. That person is being abstemious.

The single most important word here is deliberately. A person isn't abstemious simply because they happen to eat little. They're abstemious because they make a conscious, disciplined choice to restrain themselves.

Abstemious is most commonly used about food and drink — especially alcohol. But it can also describe a generally restrained, simple way of living: someone who avoids excessive pleasures, comfort, or luxury across the board.

You can use it to describe a person, their habits, or their lifestyle:

  • "He is an abstemious man."
  • "Her abstemious eating habits impressed everyone."
  • "They led an abstemious life."

Abstemious is almost always a compliment, or at the very least neutral. It quietly signals discipline, self-control, and wisdom — the strength to hold back where others don't. When you call someone abstemious, there's a note of quiet respect in it.

Very occasionally, in certain contexts, it can carry a faint suggestion of "overly strict" or "joyless," but this is rare. The dominant tone is admiration for self-restraint.
How it's different from similar words

This is where precision matters most.

Abstemious vs. Temperate / Moderate — These also mean "not going to extremes," but they're vaguer and broader. Abstemious is more specifically rooted in food and drink, and it implies a more visible, deliberate pulling-back. A "temperate" person is balanced across many areas of life. An "abstemious" person is particularly and noticeably sparing about what they consume.

Abstemious vs. Abstinent — Abstinent is stronger. It means you completely avoid something — a person abstinent from alcohol drinks none at all. Abstemious doesn't mean zero; it means very little, by deliberate choice. Someone abstemious might have a single small glass of wine. Someone abstinent skips it entirely.

Abstemious vs. Frugal — Frugal is specifically about money and spending, not food or drink. Don't mix these up.

Abstemious vs. Ascetic — An ascetic person takes self-denial to a far greater extreme, often for spiritual or moral reasons — giving up all comfort, pleasure, and ease. Abstemious is much milder. You can be abstemious and still enjoy life comfortably. An ascetic might sleep on a hard floor and eat plain bread as a practice.

Abstemious vs. Spartan — Spartan describes a tough, no-frills, stripped-down lifestyle overall. It's stronger and broader in scope than abstemious.

Think of it as a sliding scale of restraint:

Moderate → Abstemious → Abstinent → Ascetic

Abstemious sits in the middle: more deliberate and noticeable than simply being "moderate," but nowhere near extreme.
Sentences to see it in action

1. "Despite the enormous holiday spread, Uncle Ray was abstemious as ever — one small plate, one glass of water, done."
  2. "Her abstemious habits at the dinner table were well known; she always took the smallest portions and never went back for seconds."
  3. "He lived an abstemious life: no alcohol, simple meals, and no appetite for luxury."
  4. "Even at the wine-tasting event, she remained abstemious, barely letting each wine reach her lips before setting the glass aside."
  5. "The doctor admired her patient's abstemious approach to eating — it had kept his cholesterol in check for a decade."
One thing to keep in mind

Abstemious is a formal word. You're far more likely to encounter it in books, formal writing, journalism, or educated speech than in everyday casual conversation. If you're texting a friend, you'd probably just say "he barely touched the food." But in an essay, a speech, or a formal context, abstemious fits beautifully — and using it precisely marks you as someone who commands language well.
114:
Abstention means the deliberate, conscious choice to hold yourself back from doing something — especially something you are fully able to do, entitled to do, or even expected to do.

The single most important thing to understand about abstention is that it is active, not passive. It is not the same as forgetting, being absent, or being prevented from something. When someone abstains, they are present, capable, and aware — but they make a clear, intentional decision to step back and not participate.

A simple way to picture it: if someone offers you a piece of cake and you simply weren't in the room, you didn't abstain — you were just absent. But if the cake is right in front of you, you could eat it, yet you deliberately say "no, I'm choosing not to" — that is abstention. You had the full opportunity; you made a conscious choice to pass it up.

This is by far the most common and important context for this word. In any formal vote — in a parliament, a committee, a board meeting, or an international body like the United Nations — each eligible voter generally has three options: vote yes (in favor), vote no (against), or abstain.

An abstention here means a voter is present and fully entitled to vote, but chooses not to cast a vote for either side. It is a formal, recognized third option — and critically, it is not the same as simply being absent or not showing up to the vote. The person showed up; they just chose not to pick a side.

People abstain in a vote for a variety of reasons. They might feel they don't have enough information to make a fair and informed judgment. They might have a personal conflict of interest — meaning they have something to personally gain or lose from the outcome — and feel it would be inappropriate for them to take a side. They might disagree with how a question is being framed and feel that voting yes or no would misrepresent their actual position. Or they might be sending a deliberate political signal — expressing dissatisfaction or neutrality without going as far as outright opposing something.

It's also worth knowing that an abstention is never truly "neutral" in its real-world effect. In many formal bodies, the rules determine whether abstentions count toward the total votes needed to pass a decision. So depending on the system, an abstention can influence the outcome just as surely as a yes or no vote — just in a more indirect way. This is exactly why abstentions in major votes — such as those in the United Nations Security Council — are closely watched and considered politically meaningful.

Outside of voting, abstention describes the deliberate choice to hold back from a specific activity, usually one that is tempting, pleasurable, or habitual.

If a person who enjoys alcohol goes to a party and consciously chooses not to drink, they are practicing abstention from alcohol. If someone on a diet resists dessert despite wanting it, that is an abstention from sugar. If a person stays silent during a heated argument even though they have plenty they could say, that is an abstention from speech.

The common thread in all these cases is self-restraint combined with willpower. The person could do the thing — nothing is stopping them from the outside. But they choose, entirely of their own will, not to do it.

These two words are closely related and often confused, so understanding the difference is worthwhile.

Abstinence refers to an ongoing, usually long-term or even permanent commitment to avoiding something. It often relates to physical pleasures or deeply ingrained habits — like abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, or sexual activity. It implies a sustained, lifestyle-level choice rather than a one-off decision.

Abstention tends to refer to a single act or specific instance of refraining — especially in a formal, situational context like a vote or a particular moment of temptation.

A rough way to remember the distinction: abstinence is a way of living, while abstention is more often a single act or decision in a given moment. That said, in casual everyday speech, the two words are sometimes used interchangeably, and the distinction isn't always rigidly maintained outside of formal writing or legal contexts.

Knowing the related forms of the word helps you recognize and use it naturally in different sentences.

Abstain is the verb — the action word. ("She chose to abstain from the vote." / "He abstained from eating processed food all month.")

Abstaining is the present participle, used for ongoing action. ("Three members are abstaining from the decision.")

Abstained is the past tense. ("The delegate abstained during the final round of voting.")

Abstentions is the plural noun form. ("There were five abstentions recorded in the final count.")

Abstention is the deliberate, intentional act of not doing something you could do — most powerfully used when talking about voting (choosing neither yes nor no as a formal position) and in personal behavior (consciously choosing to hold back from an activity or temptation). Its defining quality is always intentionality: abstention is never an accident or an oversight. It is a choice made by someone who is fully capable of participating but decides, for their own reasons, not to.
115:
Abstinence means the deliberate, conscious choice to hold yourself back from doing something — especially something that is pleasurable, tempting, or that you are capable of doing — either for a period of time or permanently.

The single most important thing to understand about abstinence is that it is always voluntary. A person who can't afford alcohol isn't practicing abstinence from alcohol. A person who chooses not to drink alcohol, even though they could, is. The choice is the heart of the word.

Think of it this way: abstinence isn't about inability. It's about willpower meeting a deliberate decision.

Abstinence is a broad word. While it is most commonly heard in a few specific contexts, it can technically apply to choosing to hold back from almost anything.

The most common uses are:

1. Sexual abstinence — This is by far the most frequent context in which you'll encounter the word. It refers to the choice to not engage in sexual activity. This is often discussed in health education, religious settings, and relationship conversations. When someone simply says "abstinence" without any further context, this is usually what they mean.

2. Abstinence from alcohol — Choosing to not drink alcohol at all, as opposed to simply drinking less. Someone who gives up alcohol entirely is practicing abstinence from it.

3. Abstinence from drugs — Similarly, choosing to completely stop using recreational or addictive substances.

4. Abstinence from food — When someone fasts — say, for religious or health reasons — they are practicing a form of abstinence from food (or from specific foods).

5. Broader applications — In a less formal sense, someone could talk about abstinence from social media, gambling, or any other behavior they are intentionally cutting out of their life.

Abstinence is most powerfully used when it means complete avoidance. If a recovering alcoholic stops drinking entirely, that is full abstinence. If they simply drink less, that would more accurately be called moderation — not abstinence.

That said, you may sometimes hear the phrase partial abstinence, which refers to cutting out only certain aspects of something. For example, someone might practice partial abstinence from meat by giving up red meat but still eating fish. This usage is less common and is always clearly labeled as "partial."

Unless stated otherwise, assume abstinence = complete avoidance.

Abstinence can be either:

  • Temporary — "I'm practicing abstinence from sugar for the month of January."
  • Permanent — "After recovering from addiction, she committed to lifelong abstinence from drugs."

Neither version is more "correct." The word works in both situations. Context will tell you which one is meant.

Understanding the reasons helps cement the meaning. People choose abstinence for a wide range of motivations:

  • Religious or moral beliefs — Many religions encourage abstinence from sex before marriage, or from certain foods or alcohol.
  • Health reasons — A doctor might advise abstinence from alcohol to protect the liver, or from certain foods to manage a condition.
  • Personal goals — Someone trying to break a bad habit or addiction might commit to abstinence to regain control of their life.
  • Ethical reasons — A person might abstain from certain foods or products for ethical or environmental reasons.

The reason behind the abstinence doesn't change the word's meaning, but it gives it human richness.

Since this word has a useful family around it, knowing them will help you recognize and use abstinence more confidently:

  • Abstain (verb) — the action. "She decided to abstain from voting." "He abstains from meat."
  • Abstinent (adjective) — describing someone who practices abstinence. "He has been abstinent for three years."
  • Abstainer (noun, person) — someone who abstains. "She is a lifelong abstainer from alcohol."
How Abstinence Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close neighbors to abstinence, and knowing the difference sharpens your understanding:

  • Celibacy — This specifically means abstinence from sex and is almost always tied to religious or spiritual commitment (e.g., a monk's vow of celibacy). Abstinence is the broader, more neutral word; celibacy is a specific, often permanent, religiously motivated form of sexual abstinence.
  • Sobriety — This refers specifically to abstaining from alcohol (and sometimes drugs). A sober person is abstinent from alcohol, but "sobriety" carries a strong cultural and emotional weight around recovery from addiction. You wouldn't say someone is practicing "sobriety" from sugar.
  • Fasting — This is abstinence from food or drink, typically for a defined period and often for religious or health reasons. Fasting is a type of abstinence, not a synonym for it.
  • Self-control / Restraint — These are broader character traits. Abstinence is one specific expression of self-control. A person with great self-control might practice abstinence, but self-control covers far more ground — like keeping your temper or resisting the urge to interrupt someone.
How to Use Abstinence in a Sentence

Here are natural, real-world examples to see the word in action:

  • "The doctor recommended complete abstinence from alcohol during the treatment."
  • "The program teaches teenagers about sexual abstinence as one option in health education."
  • "After years of struggle, his abstinence from drugs has lasted over a decade."
  • "She practices abstinence from social media every Sunday to rest her mind."
  • "The religious tradition calls for abstinence from meat on certain days of the year."

If you had to carry just one idea away: abstinence is a chosen, deliberate decision to completely hold back from something you are capable of doing — most often something pleasurable — whether for health, moral, religious, or personal reasons, and for any length of time.
116:
Abstinent means deliberately choosing to stay away from something — usually something that gives pleasure or satisfaction — through personal self-control. A person who is abstinent can do something, but chooses not to.

That last part is crucial. Abstinent is never about inability. It is always about a conscious, willing choice to hold back.

Three things are almost always true when this word applies:

1. There is desire or temptation involved.
You wouldn't call someone "abstinent" from eating sand, because no one wants to eat sand. The word only makes sense when the thing being avoided is something the person could enjoy or be drawn to — alcohol, food, drugs, sex, and so on.

2. The choice is voluntary.
No one forces an abstinent person to hold back. They make the decision themselves, often out of willpower, values, health reasons, religious belief, or personal goals.

3. It is ongoing, not just a one-time moment.
Saying "no" to a drink once at a party is just a choice. Being abstinent means you have made a sustained, consistent commitment to avoid something over a period of time.

"Abstinent" is most commonly used in four areas:

Alcohol and drugs. This is perhaps the most frequent usage. Someone who does not drink alcohol at all — especially someone recovering from addiction — is described as abstinent. "She has been abstinent from alcohol for three years."

Food. Someone who avoids certain foods for health, religious, or ethical reasons can be called abstinent. Fasting during a religious period, for example, makes a person temporarily abstinent from food. "During Lent, he remained abstinent from meat."

Sexual activity. A person who chooses not to engage in sexual activity — for any reason, whether religious, personal, or otherwise — is described as sexually abstinent. "They chose to be abstinent until marriage."

General use. Though less common, the word can describe restraint from anything — social media, gambling, caffeine, or any habit. "Staying abstinent from her phone in the evenings helped her sleep better."
A Key Nuance: Total vs. Partial

When someone is completely abstinent, they avoid the thing entirely — not even a sip, not even once.

When someone is partially abstinent, they have significantly cut back and mostly avoid something, but not with perfect completeness. However, be aware: in strict medical and clinical use (especially with alcohol and drug recovery), "abstinent" almost always means total avoidance. If a doctor says a patient must be "abstinent," they mean zero — none whatsoever.

It is easy to mix this word up with others. Here is how it is different:

  • Abstinent ≠ Moderate. A moderate drinker has a drink occasionally but in small amounts. An abstinent person does not drink at all. Moderation is about limiting; abstinence is about stopping entirely.
  • Abstinent ≠ Forced to stop. If someone cannot drink because of a severe allergy, they are not "abstinent" — they are simply unable to. Abstinent always means choosing to stop when you physically could do it.
  • Abstinent ≠ Indifferent. If you have never tried alcohol and feel no pull toward it, calling yourself "abstinent" would be odd. The word carries the sense of resisting something that has some appeal or relevance to you.

Since you will encounter these in the wild, here are the related forms:

  • Abstain (verb) — the action. "She decided to abstain from voting."
  • Abstinence (noun) — the state or practice of being abstinent. "His abstinence from alcohol improved his health."
  • Abstainer (noun) — a person who abstains. "He is a lifelong abstainer."
  • Abstinent (adjective) — describes the person or their state. "She remained abstinent throughout the program."

If you had to distill this word to its soul, it would be this:

An abstinent person is someone who, through their own willpower and choice, consistently stays away from something pleasurable or tempting.

It is a word that carries quiet strength — the idea that a person has made a firm, deliberate decision and is sticking to it. Whether it is alcohol, food, sex, or any other indulgence, being abstinent means saying "no" not because you must, but because you have decided to.
117:
The best way to understand "abstract" is to start with its opposite: concrete. A concrete thing is something real, physical, and tangible — something you can experience directly through your senses. A dog is concrete. A chair is concrete. Rain, fire, a apple, a broken bone — all concrete. You can touch them, see them, smell them, or hear them. They exist out there in the physical world, independent of your thoughts.

An abstract thing, by contrast, exists only as an idea or concept in the mind. It has no physical form. You cannot hold it, see it, or point to it directly. Think of words like love, justice, freedom, courage, democracy, beauty, time, truth, evil, infinity. These things are genuinely real and meaningful — but they don't exist as physical objects. You can see a person acting bravely, but you cannot see "courage" itself floating around in the room. You can observe a fair trial, but you cannot touch "justice." The concept lives in thought and language, not in the physical world.

This is the heart of the word: abstract = existing in thought, not in physical reality.
The Spectrum from Concrete to Abstract

One of the most important things to understand is that "abstract" is not a simple yes-or-no category. It is a spectrum, and you can move along it in degrees.

Consider this chain: Labrador → dog → animal → living thing → existence. Each step moves you further from the concrete and deeper into the abstract. "Labrador" is very concrete — you can picture a specific animal. "Dog" is slightly more general. "Animal" is even broader. "Living thing" is broader still. And "existence" is so general and removed from any specific physical thing that it is highly abstract. As you move up the chain, you strip away more and more specific, physical details and deal increasingly with pure concepts.

This is why abstract ideas are often harder to define than concrete ones. If someone asks "what is a chair?" you can simply point to one. If someone asks "what is justice?" you cannot point — you have to think, reason, and use other words to explain it. That difficulty is a signature of abstraction.
Degrees of Abstraction in Everyday Life

You encounter abstract and concrete things constantly, often without noticing the difference.

The number "5" is abstract. You can have 5 apples (concrete), 5 people (concrete), 5 seconds (somewhat abstract), but the number 5 itself — as a pure mathematical concept — has no physical form. Mathematics is almost entirely abstract, which is part of why children often find it difficult: they are being asked to work with pure ideas before they have enough experience with physical examples.

Emotions are abstract. You can see the physical signs of someone being angry — a flushed face, a raised voice, clenched fists — but "anger" itself, as a feeling and a concept, is abstract. It lives in the inner world of experience and mind.

Moral and social concepts are heavily abstract: rights, responsibility, fairness, dignity, guilt, honour. These concepts shape human society enormously, yet none of them are physical things. You cannot weigh "honour" on a scale.

Time is interestingly abstract. You can see a clock (concrete), but time itself — the concept of duration, of past and future — is abstract. Philosophers and physicists have argued about its true nature for centuries, precisely because it cannot simply be pointed at.

You may also hear the word used in the context of art. Abstract art is art that does not attempt to depict or represent recognisable real-world objects, people, or scenes. Instead, it uses shapes, colours, lines, and forms to express ideas, emotions, or purely aesthetic experiences. When you look at an abstract painting, you might not be able to say "that is a tree" or "that is a face" — and that is the point. The artist is working directly with concepts or feelings rather than with realistic images of physical things. The word carries the same core meaning: removed from the concrete, physical world and operating at the level of idea or feeling.

When someone says a person is good at "abstract thinking," they mean that person is able to reason about concepts and ideas beyond specific, concrete examples. A child who can only understand "3" by counting three actual physical objects is thinking concretely. A person who understands "3" as a general, universal concept that applies to anything — and can manipulate it in their mind without needing physical objects — is thinking abstractly. Abstract thinking allows you to generalise, to spot patterns across different situations, to understand principles, and to reason about things you cannot directly observe.

Many people assume that because something is abstract, it must be vague, unimportant, or impractical. This is wrong. Abstract concepts are among the most powerful and consequential things humans deal with. Wars have been fought over abstract ideas like freedom and justice. Civilisations are built on abstract concepts like law, rights, and morality. Mathematics — almost entirely abstract — is the foundation of all modern science and technology. The fact that something is abstract simply means it exists as an idea rather than a physical object. It says nothing about whether it is important, meaningful, or real.

So, when you see the word "abstract" used as an adjective, ask yourself: can this thing be physically touched, seen, or directly experienced through the senses? If yes, it leans concrete. If no — if it exists primarily as a concept, idea, principle, or quality in the mind — it is abstract. The more removed something is from any specific, physical, sensory reality, the more abstract it is. And the more it deals with pure thought, general principles, or invisible qualities, the deeper into abstraction it goes.
118: "Abstract" as a noun has two core meanings — one very practical and widely used, the other more philosophical. You'll also encounter a third, narrower meaning in art. Here's everything you need to know about all three.
Meaning 1: A Short Summary of a Longer Document

This is the most common and important meaning, especially in academic, scientific, and professional life.

An abstract is a brief, condensed summary of a longer piece of writing — most often a research paper, scientific study, academic article, or legal document. It appears at the very top of the document, before the main content begins, and it is short — typically between 100 and 300 words, no matter how long the full document is.

Think of it this way. Imagine a scientist spends two years researching the effects of sleep deprivation on memory, then writes a 60-page paper about it. Now, thousands of other researchers around the world might be looking for studies on this very topic. They cannot read 60 pages of every single paper they come across — they don't have the time. So the scientist writes a short paragraph at the beginning of the paper that tells you:

  • What the study was about
  • What question it tried to answer
  • How the research was carried out
  • What was found
  • What conclusion was reached

That paragraph is the abstract. It is the whole paper squeezed into a tiny space — enough for a reader to decide whether the full paper is worth reading.

A well-written abstract is self-contained. This means you can fully understand it without reading the rest of the document. It does not leave things unexplained or say things like "as discussed below." It stands on its own.

Examples in use:

  • "The journal requires every submitted paper to include an abstract of no more than 250 words."
  • "I skimmed through the abstracts of twenty studies before finding the one I needed."
  • "Her abstract was so clear and well-written that I immediately wanted to read the full paper."

One important distinction: An abstract is not the same as an introduction. An introduction is part of the full document and leads the reader into the topic. An abstract stands apart from the document and gives a complete bird's-eye view of it. Also, an abstract never contains new information — it only reflects what is already inside the full document.
Meaning 2: A Pure Idea, Separated from Reality

The second meaning is more philosophical, and you will most often encounter it through the phrase "in the abstract."

When something is discussed in the abstract, it means you are thinking about it purely as a concept or idea — in theory, in general terms — without connecting it to any specific real situation, person, or example.

The idea here is that you are lifting a concept out of the messy, complicated real world and examining it in its cleanest, most ideal form.

Example: Imagine two people discussing the idea of fairness.

  • Discussing it in the abstract means talking about what fairness means as a concept — what a perfectly fair world would look like, what the definition of fairness is, how it works in theory.
  • Discussing it in the concrete (the opposite) means talking about a specific real situation — "Was it fair that Maria got promoted but not James?"

The phrase "in the abstract" often appears when someone wants to point out that something sounds good in theory but may not work in practice.

Examples in use:

  • "In the abstract, free healthcare for everyone sounds like a wonderful idea — but the real challenge is how to fund it."
  • "He could discuss courage beautifully in the abstract, but when the moment of crisis came, he froze."
  • "The law makes sense in the abstract, but applying it to real cases is far more complicated."

You may also hear the plural — "abstracts" or the related word "abstraction" — used to refer to ideas and concepts that have no physical form. Things like justice, freedom, love, truth, beauty are abstracts. You cannot hold them in your hand or point to them in a room. They exist only as ideas. This contrasts with concrete things — a chair, a person, a cup of coffee — things that exist in physical reality.
Meaning 3: A Work of Abstract Art

In art, an abstract (or "an abstract") can refer to a piece of artwork that does not try to depict real-world things — people, landscapes, objects — in a realistic way. Instead, it uses shapes, colors, textures, and forms to express something more emotional or conceptual.

This use of "abstract" as a standalone noun is less common. You're more likely to hear people say "an abstract painting" or "abstract art" (where "abstract" acts as an adjective). But saying "That painting is an abstract" is perfectly correct and understood.

Example in use:

  • "The gallery's new collection features several large abstracts by up-and-coming artists."
The Thread That Connects All Three Meanings

Notice what all three meanings share: the idea of moving away from the specific and physical, toward something more condensed, general, or conceptual.

  • In Meaning 1, an abstract takes a large, specific document and reduces it to its pure essence.
  • In Meaning 2, discussing something "in the abstract" means lifting it away from specific real-world situations into the realm of pure thought.
  • In Meaning 3, abstract art moves away from depicting specific real things and instead works with pure form and feeling.

Once you see this common thread, the word becomes intuitive — and you'll never confuse or forget it again.
119: Abstract Expressionism is an art movement where artists use non-recognizable shapes, colors, and marks — rather than pictures of real things — to express raw inner emotions, unconscious thoughts, and psychological states.
Breaking Down the Two Words

"Abstract" means the artwork does not show recognizable things from the real world — no portraits, no landscapes, no bowls of fruit. Instead, you see shapes, lines, colors, drips, and gestures that don't look like anything specific.

"Expressionism" means the purpose of the art is to express something felt deeply on the inside — an emotion, a mood, a psychological state — rather than to depict or document the outside world.

Put them together: Abstract Expressionism is art that uses non-representational visual elements (shapes, color, line, texture) to express something deeply emotional or psychological.
Where Did It Come From?

Abstract Expressionism was the first major art movement born in the United States. It emerged in New York City roughly between the 1940s and the mid-1950s, and it grew out of a very specific historical atmosphere.

World War II had just devastated the world. The Holocaust had happened. The atomic bomb had been dropped. Artists were grappling with profound anxiety, moral horror, and existential uncertainty. Old ways of picturing the world felt inadequate. How do you paint the feeling of post-war dread? You can't just draw a sad face. That felt too shallow, too easy.

At the same time, many European artists — especially the Surrealists (who were fascinated by dreams and the unconscious mind) — had fled Nazi-occupied Europe and landed in New York. Their ideas about tapping into the unconscious heavily influenced the American artists who would become Abstract Expressionists.

The movement was also shaped by Jungian psychology — the idea that all humans share a deep layer of unconscious experience, and that powerful symbols and primal emotions live beneath our rational surface. Many abstract expressionists believed that if they could access and express that level, their art would strike a universal chord in any viewer.
The Two Main Styles Within the Movement

Abstract Expressionism is not one single look. It has two broad tendencies, and understanding both makes the whole picture much clearer.

1. Action Painting (Gestural Abstraction)

Here, the physical act of painting is itself the expression. The artist's body is directly involved — the sweep of an arm, the flick of a wrist, the energy of movement. The canvas becomes a kind of arena in which the artist "acts."

The most famous example is Jackson Pollock, who laid canvases flat on the floor and dripped, poured, flung, and splattered paint over them while moving around and even across the canvas. The resulting work is a record of his physical motion, energy, and psychological state during the process of making it. There are no planned shapes — the painting records a performance of feeling.

Franz Kline made huge, bold black brushstrokes on white canvas — not calligraphy, not writing, just raw, powerful gestures that feel architectural and urgent.

Willem de Kooning used violent, aggressive, slashing brushwork — especially in his controversial "Woman" series, which depicted distorted female figures with feverish, energetic paint handling.

The key idea here: process matters as much as — or more than — the finished product. The painting is evidence of an emotional and physical event.

2. Color Field Painting

This is quieter, more contemplative, and more meditative. Instead of frantic gesture, you get vast areas of pure, flat, luminous color. The idea is that color alone, at a large enough scale, can generate deep emotional or even spiritual experiences in the viewer without any imagery at all.

Mark Rothko is the most celebrated example. His paintings typically show two or three large, soft-edged rectangles of color floating on a colored background — nothing else. They look deceptively simple, but standing in front of a large Rothko in person, many viewers report feeling moved to tears, a sense of the sublime, even a spiritual encounter. Rothko wanted his colors to envelop you.

Barnett Newman painted what he called "zips" — vertical lines dividing large fields of color. He believed these could evoke a feeling of the infinite and the primal.

Clyfford Still used jagged, flame-like areas of color that seem to tear open the canvas, creating a raw, primordial energy.

The key idea here: pure color, at human scale, bypasses the intellect and speaks directly to emotion.
What Were These Artists Actually Trying to Express?

This is crucial. Abstract Expressionism was not random or meaningless. The artists had serious intentions:

Emotional authenticity. They wanted to reach beyond polished, controlled, "pretty" art and create something raw and genuinely felt. Slick technique was suspicious to them — it could hide real feeling.

The unconscious mind. Influenced by Freud and Jung, many believed the deepest truths about human experience live in our unconscious. Spontaneity, accident, and improvisation were tools to bypass rational control and let the unconscious speak through the artwork.

Universal human experience. They weren't trying to illustrate their personal emotions — they were after something larger. Rothko, for example, explicitly said he wasn't interested in color or shapes per se, but in expressing basic human emotions: tragedy, ecstasy, doom. He wanted anyone who looked at his paintings to experience those emotions directly.

Spiritual and philosophical questions. Many of these artists were wrestling with big questions: What does it mean to be human? How do we find meaning after such catastrophic violence? Art, for them, was a way to confront these questions honestly.
How to Recognize Abstract Expressionism

When you look at a painting and ask "Is this Abstract Expressionism?", here are the signs:

No recognizable imagery (mostly — de Kooning is a partial exception). You won't see a house, a person, a tree.

Evidence of the artist's hand and body. Visible, energetic brushstrokes, drips, splatters, or raw paint application. This is not polished academic painting.

Large scale. Abstract Expressionist canvases are often enormous — sometimes filling an entire wall. This is intentional. A large-scale work surrounds you, makes you a participant rather than a distant observer.

Emotional intensity. Even if you can't explain why, these paintings are designed to make you feel something — whether it's energy, anxiety, calm, awe, grief, or exhilaration.

Focus on the surface and material of the paint itself. The texture, weight, layering, and physical quality of the paint is part of the meaning.
The Major Artists at a Glance

Jackson Pollock — Drip paintings made by flinging paint from above. The most iconic figure of the movement.

Mark Rothko — Luminous, soft rectangles of color. Deeply meditative and emotionally overwhelming in person.

Willem de Kooning — Energetic, slashing brushwork. Bridged figuration and abstraction.

Franz Kline — Massive, bold black-and-white gestures. Looks almost architectural.

Barnett Newman — Fields of pure color divided by thin vertical lines ("zips"). Philosophical and monumental.

Lee Krasner — A major figure often overshadowed because she was Pollock's wife; her own gestural work is equally powerful.

Robert Motherwell — Known for his "Elegy to the Spanish Republic" series — recurring black oval shapes on white, a meditation on grief and loss.

Hans Hofmann — A teacher as much as a painter; he shaped many of the movement's ideas through his influential school in New York.
Why Does It Matter? The Historical Impact

Abstract Expressionism was a revolution for several reasons.

It moved the art world's center from Paris to New York. For centuries, Paris had been the undisputed capital of modern art. Abstract Expressionism was the first American art movement to be taken seriously on the world stage, and New York became the new center of the art world — a position it largely still holds.

It permanently expanded what art is allowed to be. Before this movement, even the most avant-garde art was still largely about something you could point to. Abstract Expressionism proved that art didn't need to represent anything — it could communicate directly through pure form, color, and gesture.

It opened the door to almost everything that came after. Pop Art, Minimalism, Conceptual Art, Color Field Painting, Performance Art — virtually every major art movement of the late 20th century defined itself in relationship to Abstract Expressionism, either building on it or reacting against it.

It elevated the status of American culture. In the Cold War era, the U.S. government and institutions actually promoted Abstract Expressionism internationally as proof of American creative freedom — a pointed contrast to the state-controlled "Socialist Realist" art of the Soviet Union. (This political dimension is controversial and was not something the artists themselves signed up for, but it's part of the historical record.)
The Most Common Objection — and Why It Misses the Point

Almost everyone, when first seeing Abstract Expressionist art, thinks: "My kid could do that."

This is an understandable reaction, but it misses something important. A few points:

Intent and context are everything. When your child drips paint on a page, they are not asking profound questions about consciousness, grief, the nature of art, or the human condition. When Pollock dripped paint, he was doing exactly that — with every gesture shaped by decades of thinking, a deep knowledge of art history, and deliberate psychological intent.

Skill shows up differently. In traditional art, skill is visible in rendering — does the face look real? In Abstract Expressionism, skill shows up in compositional control, emotional coherence, and the ability to sustain tension and energy across a large surface. A Pollock drip painting is actually extremely difficult to replicate successfully — countless imitators have proven that.

You don't have to "get" every artwork. Some people deeply connect with Rothko and find the experience almost spiritual. Others find it baffling. Both reactions are honest and fine. What's worth resisting is dismissing the entire project without engaging with it seriously.
Its Legacy Today

Abstract Expressionism's influence never really ended — it just transformed. You see it in:

Contemporary abstract painting, which continues in conversation with it. The raw emotional directness of the movement influenced generations of painters worldwide. Graphic designers and digital artists use color field principles constantly. The movement's insistence that process and gesture carry meaning has shaped performance art, street art, and even the aesthetics of contemporary photography and film. The idea that art should reach for authentic emotional expression over polished technique is now almost universally accepted in modern creative culture.
The Summary You Can Always Return To

Abstract Expressionism = an American art movement (1940s–50s, New York) where artists rejected representational imagery in favor of using shape, color, and physical gesture to express profound emotions, unconscious psychological states, and universal human experience. It has two main branches: Action Painting (energetic, gestural, process-driven — think Pollock) and Color Field Painting (meditative, color-driven, sublime — think Rothko). It was the first American art movement to reshape global art history, and its core conviction — that pure visual form can communicate deep inner truth without depicting the outside world — permanently changed what art is.
